title: Given an array of numbers and a value k, find the kth largest element efficiently using a priority queue (heap).
shortTitle: Find the Kth Largest Element Using a Min-Heap
keyPoints: Maintain a min-heap of size k; the root is always the kth largest element seen so far.
For each element, offer it to the heap, and if the heap exceeds size k, poll the smallest out.
After processing all n elements, the heap's root is the kth largest overall.
Time is O(n log k) and space is O(k), which beats full sorting at O(n log n) when k is small.
The heap approach works on streams because you never need all n elements in memory.
Quickselect is the expected-linear in-memory alternative but has a quadratic worst case and cannot stream.

s1_definition.oneliner: Keep the k largest in a size-k min-heap, and its root is the kth largest, in O(n log k) time.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Min-heap of size k** – Java's `PriorityQueue` is a min-heap by default, with `peek` returning the smallest.
- **Offer and poll** – for each element, offer it; if size exceeds k, poll the smallest out.
- **Root is answer** – after processing all elements, `peek()` returns the kth largest.
- **O(n log k) time** – each offer and poll on a size-k heap is O(log k), done n times.
- **O(k) space** – only k elements are held at any time, enabling stream processing.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants the third-largest transaction of the day from a stream of thousands. A clerk keeps a small tray that holds only the three biggest seen so far, arranged so the smallest of those three is at the front. For each new transaction, if it is bigger than the front, she replaces the front one. At the end, the front of the tray is exactly the third-largest.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The kth largest element is the value at position k from the top when the array is sorted descending. The brute-force way is to sort and index, but the min-heap approach is better when k is small or the data is a stream. I maintain a min-heap of size k so the root is always the smallest of the k largest seen so far, and after processing all elements the root is the kth largest overall.

In Java the heap is a PriorityQueue, which is a min-heap by default. I offer every element, and if the heap exceeds size k, I poll to discard the smallest. The time is O(n log k) with O(k) space, and it works on streams because I never hold more than k elements.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this in a reporting dashboard that surfaces the top few largest transactions from a high-volume stream without storing the entire feed.

The senior-level trade-off is between the min-heap and Quickselect. The heap is deterministic, stream-friendly, and O(n log k). Quickselect is expected-linear but has a quadratic worst case and cannot stream.

Remember one sentence: a size-k min-heap discards everything too small and its root is the kth largest.
